editorialDecl.p: The sūtra text is that of Ānandajoti Bhikkhu's typed edition of Kedāranātha's printed text, extracted from the text layer of his PDF. The transliteration has been converted from IAST to ISO 15919 (ṛ > r̥, e > ē, o > ō; ṁ was already used); the text is otherwise as typed, including hyphens marking word boundaries within compounds and the typist's irregularities. The "// n:m //" sūtra numbers are encoded as the position of the sūtra within its adhyāya (@n and @xml:id). Two sūtras are numbered 6:7 in the source; they are Pi.6.7a (printed in square brackets in the original edition) and Pi.6.7b.

Everything that Ānandajoti Bhikkhu added is marked resp="#AB": captions between sūtras (the square-bracketed headings, here ab[@type="caption"]), metre names given after a sūtra number (note[@type="metre-name"]), metrical schemes (note[@type="scheme"], rows separated by lb), other square-bracketed remarks (note[@type="comment"]) and footnotes. His preface is in front. Page breaks (pb) follow the page numbers in the running head of his PDF.

glyph.desc: Metrical symbol used by Ānandajoti Bhikkhu for the gaṇa positions of the Āryā family that are shown as ⏑ over a lowered −, followed by ⏑ (rendered as a ligature in his font); it has no Unicode character and is stored at U+F804 in the PDF.

div.head: Preface to this Edition
div.p: This edition of Chandaḥśāstram is essentially a transliteration of the sūtras that are found in the Kāvyamālā Series, Vol 91 (Bombay, 1938), where the full title is given as:
div.quote:
The Chhandas Śāstra
by Śrī Piṁgalanāga.
With the Commentary Mr̥itasañjīvanī,
by Śrī Halāyudha Bhaṭṭa.
With the Chhandonirukti by
Samīkṣāchakravartī Śrī Madhusūdana Vidyāvāchaspati.
Edited by Paṇḍit Kedāranāth of Jaipur.
Third Edition.
Revised with notes by
Vidyālaṅkār Anant Yajneśvar Śāstrī Dhupkar.
div.p: The original work, as can be seen from the title, included the authorative commentary by Śrī Halāyudha, and what amounts to two sub-commentaries. At the moment the momumental commentaries have not been prepared, and in their place I have simply added the metrical markings, and one or two notes, when there are difficulties that need explaining.

As with Śrī Kedārabhaṭṭa’s Vr̥ttaratnākara, the immediate purpose in preparing this work has been to have a text to accompany the Pāḷi prosody Vuttodaya, which is currently in preparation, and so the amount of time I can dedicate to this work has been unfortunately limited. Even so it has thrown much light on some of the more intractable problems associated with the Pāḷi work, and a study of the text is recommended for anyone interested in Indian prosody.
